nameStory: The tiger lily gets its fierce name from its brilliant orange petals decorated with dark black spots, resembling the bold stripes and markings of a tiger's coat. When you see these dramatic flowers nodding in a garden or along a roadside, the tiger connection becomes immediately obvious—it's nature's own wild cat prowling through the flower world.
description: Tiger lily is a tall, showy perennial that can reach 3-6 feet in height, topped with distinctive orange flowers that seem to glow like flames. Each flower faces downward with six curved-back petals covered in dark spots, creating an unmistakable tiger-striped pattern. Originally from Asia, this garden favorite has escaped cultivation and now pops up wild throughout New England. The plant grows from a scaly underground bulb and produces a single sturdy stem lined with narrow, lance-shaped leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant orange flowers with six recurved (curved backward) petals covered in dark black spots, hanging downward like bright lanterns. The petals feel waxy and curve so far back they almost touch behind the flower, with prominent orange stamens tipped with dark pollen dangling below.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately up the stem, feeling smooth and slightly thick to the touch. Look for tiny dark bulbils (small black bulb-like structures) growing in the leaf joints along the stem—these are unique to tiger lilies.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single sturdy stem grows 3-6 feet tall from an underground scaly bulb, typically unbranched with flowers clustered at the top. The stem feels firm and slightly ridged, often with a purplish tinge.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces upright seed capsules that split open to reveal flat, papery seeds, though many tiger lilies spread primarily through the small black bulbils that drop from leaf joints rather than seeds.

habitat: Tiger lilies thrive in gardens, along roadsides, and in disturbed areas where they've escaped cultivation throughout New England. They prefer well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and are commonly found near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, and along rural roads. You'll often spot them growing in small colonies where the bulbils have dropped and established new plants nearby.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as pointed green spears pushing through the soil, quickly developing into leafy stems. The distinctive alternately-arranged leaves make identification possible even before flowering.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season from July through August, when the spectacular orange blooms are impossible to miss. This is when the black bulbils are also most visible in the leaf joints.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while the bulbils in leaf joints ripen and may drop to start new plants. Stems begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground bulb, leaving no above-ground trace. Look for dried stem remnants or small plants growing from dropped bulbils.

funFact: Tiger lilies are botanical time travelers—they rarely produce viable seeds and instead clone themselves by dropping tiny black bulbils from their leaf joints, meaning many of the tiger lilies you see today are genetically identical to plants that arrived from Asia over a century ago.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with our native wood lily, but wood lily flowers face upward like cups while tiger lily flowers hang downward like bells, and wood lily lacks the distinctive black bulbils in the leaf joints. Remember: tigers hang their heads, wood lilies look up at the sky.
contextualKnowledge: While called "tiger lily," this name is sometimes applied to other orange lilies, creating confusion. This species was formerly known scientifically as Lilium tigrinum, which you might still see in older books. It's also worth noting that tiger lilies are completely edible—the bulbs, flowers, and even the bulbils are consumed as food in many Asian cuisines.
compareHints: Among New England's lilies, tiger lily is the only one with black bulbils in the leaf joints and the only non-native species commonly encountered. Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily also have recurved petals, but both are yellow or yellow-orange rather than bright orange, and neither has the tiger's distinctive black spots or bulbils. Wood lily has orange petals but faces upward rather than downward.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's true lilies, Canada lily is the only one with consistently downward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange shades.
Unlike its relatives Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have downward-facing or nodding flowers, wood lily is the only native lily in New England that consistently faces its flowers upward.

Among New England's native lilies, Turk's-cap lily is the tallest and most dramatic, with its hanging orange flowers and completely recurved petals setting it apart from the upward-facing Canada lily and the smaller, red Wood lily.
Among New England's true lilies, Michigan lily is distinguished by its moderate height (shorter than Turk's-cap lily but taller than wood lily) and its orange color with backward-curved petals.
Unlike our native Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have drooping, downward-facing flowers, Formosa lily blooms face outward horizontally.
Unlike our native lilies, martagon lily has distinctly whorled leaves rather than alternate or scattered leaf arrangements.
